title: Google's TPUv8s for Training and Inference at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Google's eighth-gen TPU family splits into a dedicated training chip (8t) and inference chip (8i) released in the same year rather than alternated, with Google arguing its decade of building both training and inference silicon (unlike other hyperscalers who buy commodity training hardware) is a durable structural edge; the 8t superpod scales to 9,600 chips / 121 EFLOPS FP4 with 2x perf-per-watt over TPUv7 Ironwood.

themes.theme: Custom silicon strategy vs. hyperscaler peers

insights.claim: Google is unique among hyperscalers in building custom silicon for both AI training and inference simultaneously, while other hyperscalers rely on commodity (Nvidia) hardware for training and only build custom chips for inference.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: This is a structural differentiator versus AWS Trainium/Inferentia and Microsoft Maia strategies; it reduces Google's dependency on Nvidia GPUs for the highest-value training workloads, a durable moat argument for Alphabet's cloud/AI cost structure.
insights.quote: Whereas the other operators have been focused solely on developing inference hardware while relying on commodity hardware for training, Google has continued to develop their own hardware for both tasks right up to the current day.
insights.locator: Google's rate of development for their tensor processor units

insights.claim: Google claims its decade of dual training-and-inference chip design experience is itself a competitive edge in the AI silicon market, not just a cost-saving move.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: If true, this compounding design experience is hard for AWS/Microsoft/Meta to replicate quickly, supporting a long-term view that Google's silicon org has a lead in architecture maturity even if unit economics parity with Nvidia is debated.
insights.locator: This experience, Google has argued in the past

insights.claim: Google switched TPU 8i host CPUs from x86 to its own in-house Arm-based Axion CPU, pairing TPU 8i chips with Axion CPUs in a 2-to-1 ratio inside nodes.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Signals Google is vertically integrating the entire node (accelerator + host CPU), further reducing Intel/AMD x86 exposure in its AI fleet and cutting into the addressable market for merchant CPU vendors in AI racks.
insights.quote: TPU 8i chips are paired with Axion CPUs in a 2-to-1 ratio inside Google's nodes.
insights.locator: Besides providing their own internal chip design for inference

insights.claim: Google is now designing TPUs with cloud customer workloads in mind, not just its own internal workloads as in earlier TPU generations.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Points to Google Cloud pushing TPUs harder as an external monetizable product to compete with Nvidia GPU cloud instances, a potential new external revenue lever beyond internal cost avoidance.
insights.quote: At this point Google is also designing these chips to build for the world.

themes.theme: Why training and inference chips are diverging

insights.claim: Google split its eighth-generation TPU into two separate chips released in the same year (rather than alternating training/inference generations as before) because mixture-of-experts (MoE) models impose much heavier communication/network bottlenecks that a single unified design can no longer serve well.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms an industry-wide shift where MoE architectures are forcing chip designers to specialize further; investors should expect networking/interconnect IP (not just raw FLOPS) to become the differentiating spend area in next-gen AI silicon.
insights.quote: MoE in particular imposes new bottlenecks, as it involves a lot more in the way of communication/network traffic than earlier models. Scaling up FLOPS is not enough.

insights.claim: Inference chips need a much higher ratio of HBM and SRAM per unit of compute than training chips, illustrated by TPU 8i (8 HBM stacks) versus TPU 8t (6 HBM stacks) despite 8i being the smaller die.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Reinforces that inference workloads are increasingly memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound, a key reason HBM demand/pricing (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) is decoupling from raw GPU/accelerator unit counts.
insights.quote: the point is that inference needs more HBM per unit of compute. Inference also needs a higher percentage of SRAM to compute.

insights.claim: Inference cost rises sharply as per-user latency requirements tighten, illustrating the classic tradeoff where lower latency reduces achievable throughput per chip.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Useful mental model for modeling inference unit economics: providers offering low-latency inference SLAs (e.g. premium API tiers) inherently pay a throughput/cost penalty vs. batch/latency-tolerant inference.
insights.quote: Looking at the cost of inference, the price goes up quickly the lower the latency is.

insights.claim: This TPU generation is specifically optimized to handle the long context windows required by agentic AI workloads.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms hardware roadmaps across the industry are being re-oriented around agentic/long-context inference, not just chatbot-style short-context serving — a durable secular design driver for HBM capacity and network fabric investment.

insights.claim: TPU 8i uses a new 'BoardFly' network topology (8 trays of 4 TPUs, 36 groups) with a maximum of 7 hops, versus 16 hops for the previous 3D Torus topology used for training, because fly networks have lower latency which matters more for inference.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Shows Google diverging network topology choice by workload type (torus for training throughput, fly network for inference latency), a design pattern other AI silicon vendors (Nvidia's multiplane, Broadcom Thor Ultra) are also converging on — network topology specialization is becoming a key axis of AI infrastructure competition.
insights.quote: The BoardFly network for 8i has a maximum of 7 hops, versus 16 hops for the torus.

insights.claim: TPU 8i performs in-network collective operations in the ICI I/O die near the networking hardware rather than in the compute die, saving both data-transfer time and HBM access overhead.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: In-network compute/collectives offloading is a recurring theme across this Hot Chips generation (also seen in Nvidia SHARP-like approaches); it's becoming a standard technique to cut inference latency and is a differentiator investors should track across vendors' networking IP portfolios.

insights.claim: The TPU 8t 'superpod' scales to 9,600 chips with an aggregate 2PB of shared HBM memory and 121 EFLOPS of FP4 compute, at roughly 2x the performance-per-watt of the prior-generation TPUv7 (Ironwood).
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Concrete efficiency doubling generation-over-generation is a key data point for modeling Google's AI compute cost curve and capex efficiency versus Nvidia's roadmap cadence (Blackwell/Rubin).
insights.quote: this is 121 EFLOPS of FP4 compute. In terms of energy efficiency, this is around twice the perf-per-watt as the TPUv7 Ironwood.

insights.claim: Google's dedicated Virgo network architecture for TPU 8t (replacing use of the general data center network in prior generations) supports 134,000 TPUs in a single domain at 47 Pbits/second aggregate bandwidth using a two-layer switching topology.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A dedicated (not shared) cluster fabric at this scale signals Google is engineering for training clusters an order of magnitude larger than typical GPU clusters today, relevant to gauging the ceiling on frontier model training runs Google can support internally.
insights.quote: Virgo network architecture. This supports 134K TPUs in a single domain, for 47 Pbits/second of bandwidth.

insights.claim: Google uses an optical circuit switch (OCS) to dynamically reconfigure the 9,600-chip pod into arbitrary slice sizes/shapes, and to automatically drop bad chips, allocate spares, and restore from checkpoint without manual intervention.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Automated fault handling at this scale materially reduces effective downtime/wasted compute on massive training runs — a meaningful hidden efficiency lever versus static-topology GPU clusters that require manual node replacement.
insights.quote: OCS also handles bad chips, dropping chips when they go bad, allocating a spare node, restoring from a checkpoint, and then moving on.

insights.claim: Chip failure rates increase exponentially with temperature (per the Arrhenius equation, semiconductor wear roughly doubles for every 10-15C rise in operating temperature), making cooling a first-order reliability lever, not just a performance one.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Directly ties data center cooling investment (liquid cooling of optics, etc.) to cluster-level training reliability and effective uptime — relevant for evaluating cooling vendors and datacenter capex allocation as a reliability lever, not just an efficiency one.
insights.quote: Failure rates also increase exponentially with temperatures... The Arrhenius equation says that chemical degradation (and semicon wear) roughly doubles for every 10-15C increase in operating temperature.

insights.claim: For the first time, Google is liquid cooling the optics on the TPU 8t tray (previously air-cooled), alongside the compute itself.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Extending liquid cooling to optics is a sign of rising power density in optical interconnects at scale-up domains this large; relevant to liquid-cooling supply chain and optics vendors serving hyperscale AI clusters.
insights.quote: This is the first time that Google is liquid cooling their optics as well.

insights.claim: Google is using AI models to help design its own TPUs, with these models trimming power usage on TPU 8t and saving die area across both training and inference chips, enabling more compute cores to be packed in.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AI-assisted chip design compressing power/area is a recurring theme across this Hot Chips cycle (echoed by OpenAI's Jalapeno using AI/XLS for RTL); suggests a broader industry inflection where AI-driven EDA could meaningfully compress chip design cycles and cost for all custom-silicon programs, not just Google's.
insights.quote: These AI models have been able to trim the power usage of TPU 8t, as well as saving area on various bits of both the training and inference chips.

insights.claim: Google's Pallas custom kernel language lets developers write hardware-aware kernels directly in Python for best performance on both TPU 8t and 8i, while existing codebases remain fully backward compatible with the new generation.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Backward compatibility plus a lower-friction kernel language lowers the switching cost for cloud customers moving workloads onto new TPU generations — relevant to Google Cloud's ability to retain/expand TPU-based AI customers versus CUDA lock-in on Nvidia.

insights.claim: Google's overarching TPU design philosophy is tight co-design between compiler/software and hardware teams to avoid doing unnecessary work at runtime.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: This is Google's version of the 'full-stack co-design' thesis that Nvidia and OpenAI are also pushing at Hot Chips 2026 — a recurring cross-vendor theme suggesting software/hardware co-design is becoming the primary lever for AI efficiency gains industry-wide.
insights.quote: employing a strong co-design link between their software (compiler) and hardware developers in order to avoid doing any more than they have to at runtime.
